Photograph: Darren England/AAP View image in fullscreen The share of renters in regional Australia who are in housing stress is substantially higher than those in the cities, according to the latest Hilda survey, which has tracked the same households since 2001. Photograph: Darren England/AAP Housing Analysis Young Australians are staying in the family home for longer – and it’s not hard to see why Patrick Commins Housing costs are up with renters worst affected and financial stress is also growing, according to the largest survey of its type Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.01 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 10.04 EDT Share Every year, thousands of Australians answer a series of questions as part of the long-running Hilda survey. This questionnaire – more expansively known as the household, income and labour dynamics in Australia survey – has been tracking the same households since 2001. As the families have expanded over the past two decades, the survey has grown to include about 17,000 people a year in 9,000 households, offering a unique insight into Australian life in the 21st century – and how it has changed. This week, the Melbourne Institute of Applied Economic and Social Research, which manages the survey, published its annual snapshot of the social and economic trends shaping Australia. Here are six things we learned. Half of young Australians are living with their parents The trend is clear: leaving the nest has become ever harder. In 2001, 39% of people aged 18-29 were living at home with their folks. Fast forward to 2024, and that figure is just shy of 50%. Young men are more likely to live at home than women, but that gap has shrunk a bit over the 23 years. And 36% of 18- to 29-year-olds living at home in 2024 are full-time students. It’s also notable that the big shift towards staying at home happened through the first decade of the century. More of us studying for longer is one answer, but so is the mounting cost of moving out, which we’ll turn to a bit further below. A table showing the change in the percentage of people living at home in their 20s between 2001 and 2024 One group is being left behind Employment rates reached record highs in 2024, with the survey showing 84.4% of working-age men and 76% of working-age women had jobs. Aussie workers are better educated – more than half of women aged 25-44 now hold a university degree. Men are better educated now than at the start of the century, too, but in every age group women were found to be “considerably better educated than men,” the report said. But there is one group where employment outcomes have become much worse. As Kyle Peyton, a co-author of the report, says: “Men aged 25 to 44 who did not complete year 12 have become less likely to be in full-time work and more likely to be outside the labour force”. “Their full-time employment rate fell from 70% in 2001 to 63% in 2024, while the share outside the labour force rose from 12% to 22%,” Peyton says. Women who never finished high school – and did not achieve any other higher education – have also dropped out of the workforce at greater rates: from 40% in 2001, to 48% in 2024. That’s not as sharp an increase, but still much higher than for men. Graph showing the share of men aged 25 to 44 not participating in the workforce, by highest level of education Household income has trended higher this decade … The pandemic, the huge lockdown payments from governments, and the post-Covid inflationary outbreak has made for a bumpy ride. Median disposable (or after tax) household incomes peaked in 2021, before being pummelled by soaring living costs from 2022. The Hilda survey shows the typical household was earning less in 2024 than the recent peak in 2021, but more than in 2019. Looking longer term, the survey shows household incomes lifted strongly through the first decade of the century, before plateauing right up to the pandemic. A graph showing household income growth … but financial wellbeing is down Australians report lower financial wellbeing on average than they did before Covid-19, despite higher median household incomes. As Inga Lass, the lead author of the report, says “the post-pandemic shock to cost-of-living is clear”. There were declines in reported financial wellbeing across age groups between 2020 and 2024 – except for the over-65s. The survey asked five questions and asked people how well it described them from one (“not at all”) to five (“completely”). The researchers then converted this to a wellbeing score out of 100 (where the higher the number, the higher the wellbeing). The share of people who could enjoy life “not at all” or “very little” due to their money management lifted from 11.3% in 2020 to 12.7% in 2024. And in 2020, 62.1% agreed or strongly agreed that they felt on top of everyday finances; by 2024 it was 58.5%. And while 60% of people in 2020 agreed or strongly agreed they were comfortable with their current spending relative to the money coming in, that share had dropped to 53.8% in 2024. “These results imply that worsening perceptions of meeting shorter-term ‘every day’ financial outcomes explain a sizeable shift in the reported decline in financial wellbeing over the four-year period,” the report said. Graph showing average financial wellbeing scores by age group Housing costs are higher … Of course, we all know that the cost of keeping a roof over your head (and your family’s) has been a major factor in the new era of high living costs. The Hilda survey shows weekly mortgage payments – including principal and interest – jumped between 2021 and 2024 to reach new highs as the Reserve Bank jacked up interest rates. Fast forward to today, and the RBA has reversed the three rate cuts it made in 2025, which means the burden on mortgage holders is similar to when the last survey took place. The survey shows weekly private rental costs were pretty steady through the 2010s, but have since climbed higher and higher. And while overall household incomes are lower than they were in 2021, housing costs are higher – which has heaped pressure on many Australians. Graph showing housing costs for those with mortgages rising Housing stress is particularly acute for renters in the regions The Hilda survey uses the “30-40 rule” to measure housing stress. A household is in housing stress if housing costs are more than 30% of disposable household income, and the household is in the bottom 40% of households by disposable income. Among the cities, renters in Sydney are the most likely to be experiencing housing stress, with more than 31% meeting the definition in 2024 – that’s about twice the rate in Adelaide. The next toughest market is in Brisbane, with 26% of renters in housing stress. Across the mainland capital cities, one in four are in housing stress. As high as those rates are, the share of regional renters in housing stress is substantially higher at 30%, and nearly double what it was before the pandemic. In contrast, about one in 10 mortgaged owners are in housing stress, and that number has generally held steady over the past 20-plus years. Renters are more likely to suffer housing stress Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editor Explore more on these topics Housing Australian economy Australian education Interest rates Reserve Bank of Australia Rural and regional Australia Renting explainers Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed World Europe US news Americas Asia Australia Middle East Africa Inequality Global development

https://petapixel.com/2026/10/01/award-w.text: Copied! © Jan Wieczorek Polish photographer Jan Wieczorek’s striking black-and-white wildlife photo, “Urban Beavers,” is this year’s Rewilding Europe Award winner. The annual Rewilding Europe photography contest , presented by Rewilding Europe in partnership with the German Society for Nature Photography (GDT) and the European Wildlife Photographer of the Year contest, celebrates photos captured across Europe that illustrate “rewilding in motion.” “Rewilding” is a progressive approach to conservation that works to enable nature and natural processes to occur again, restoring and repairing damage caused by human activities. As Rewilding Europe says, “Nature knows best when it comes to survival and self-governance.” “Rewilding in Europe doesn’t have one single face. It can mean bringing back a species that disappeared, restoring natural processes, or simply giving nature enough space and time to recover on its own. But increasingly, it is also about learning how to share landscapes with wildlife,” says contest judge Jon A. Juarez. Rewilding Europe Award Winner Shows a Family of Beavers Thriving In a Polish City Award-winning photos like Wieczorek’s document that rewilding process as it happens out in the real world. In this case, a family of beavers in the Polish city of Olsztyn shows that people and wildlife can coexist. ‘Urban Beavers’ by Jan Wieczorek | Rewilding Europe Award There are power lines and railways and homes being built, but the beavers, with the protection of local authorities and the people who live there, are thriving. Award-winning photographer Jan Wieczorek has watched the beavers for nearly 15 years now, and carefully composed his photo to show the two worlds coming together. In the foggy, city-lit background, there’s a construction crane and a nearby road. In the foreground, a trio of beavers is busy at work. “The story behind the photograph shows that nature doesn’t always exist somewhere far away. It can thrive right next to our homes, beneath our bridges, and in the centers of our cities. By framing the housing development alongside the wetland created by the beavers, I wanted to show that it is possible for humans and wildlife to share space,” Wieczorek says. Photographer Jan Wieczorek has watched the beaver family he photographed for 15 years, and believes strongly that people and wildlife can coexist. “The winning and commended images capture the essence of how humans and wildlife can live side by side. Photography like this translates the complex relationships between humans and wildlife, ultimately helping us understand them better,” adds competition judge Viktoria Pezzei. Runner-Up Runner-up Christoph Kaula earned acclaim for a very different sort of recovery story. Kaula’s photo shows a little European hamster who is part of a research project scientists have undertaken to figure out how to save the threatened species. European hamsters have suffered greatly as farming operations have expanded across the continent, and researchers are taking a hands-on approach to saving the animals. Captive breeding, genetic analysis, and habitat management are all part of a multi-pronged approach. The beavers show that sometimes leaving animals alone is enough, but the European hamster shows that a more hands-on approach is needed to get things moving in the right direction. Runner-up — ‘Managed Revial’ by Christoph Kaula | Rewilding Europe Award “Bringing a species back is never the work of a single organization or individual — it’s a collective effort. And that also means raising awareness and communicating the importance of conservation to a much wider audience,” says Kaula. Commended Photos The judges gave special commendations to three more photos. Fabian Thorand’s photo, “Peaceful European Bison,” shows two bison resting in a Polish meadow. These animals were once extinct in Europe, but have been reintroduced and now number more than 10,000 individuals. Commended — ‘Peaceful European Bison’ by Fabian Thorand | Rewilding Europe Award “I hope to show how beautiful and peaceful coexistence with animals can be, even with such large ones. I believe it’s important to see nature not only as our environment, but as a natural habitat for wild animals that are worth protecting. Bison play a really important ecological role, but people have to learn how to live alongside them,” Thorand says. Silke Hüttche’s shot, “The Call of the Eagles,” shows white-tailed eagles in a very unusual part of northeastern Germany, Anklamer Stadtbruch. This 2,000-hectare area became a large wilderness area after a massive storm in the 1990s. The storm surge turned the area into peatland, which is now home to a rich diversity of animals. White-tailed eagles live here in greater numbers than anywhere else in Germany. Commended — ‘The Call of the Eagles’ by Silke Hüttche | Rewilding Europe Award “I have seen how the natural processes at work in Anklamer Stadtbruch have boosted the abundance and diversity of species found there. Today I know how incredibly important such new wilderness is,” the photographer explains. Lewis Jefferies’ photo, “A New Generation,” captures a National Lobster Hatchery staff member releasing young European lobsters into a tidal pool in Cornwall, England. The hatchery works with scientists, fishermen, and even restaurants to raise young lobsters and then release them into the sea. The European lobster has significant financial value, both for its meat and for its role in the local ecosystem. Many coastal communities rely heavily on these lobsters. Commended — ‘A New Generation’ by Lewis Jefferies | Rewilding Europe Award “I really hope this image will help spark interest in marine wildlife and conservation and raise awareness of the incredible conservation work being done in Cornwall to save species and habitats,” Jefferies says. Nature Can Survive if Given the Space and Time The annual Rewilding Europe Award photo contest shows that when humans either leave things alone or get involved thoughtfully, nature can recover. Sometimes nature recovers on its own, and sometimes it needs a little push, but importantly, people can make a positive difference. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more . AI (artificial intelligence) Analysis Is a job guarantee the solution to mass AI unemployment? Nick Romeo An old idea springs anew as a chorus of influential voices predicts that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude Fri 23 Oct 2026 06.00 EDT Share In a preface to his book Capitalism and Freedom, the American economist Milton Friedman famously observed that a crisis can propel once-fringe ideas into the political mainstream. “Only a crisis – actual or perceived – produces real change. When that crisis occurs, the actions that are taken depend on the ideas that are lying around,” he wrote. The job of intellectuals, thinktanks and economists, he argued, is to refine the quality of these ambient ideas, so that good ones are ready when disaster strikes. A chorus of influential voices is now predicting that AI may trigger crises of vast magnitude. Bill Gates has declared that AI will advance so rapidly that within a decade, humans will not be needed “for most things”. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has warned that the technology could cause widespread unemployment within one to five years, eliminating many positions in law, tech, finance and other white-collar professions. Even if these predictions are wrong, investors who bet heavily on the technology may conclude that AI is a bubble, and this in itself could cause a recession and widespread job loss. Whether a crisis of mass AI-related job loss turns out to be actual or perceived, one policy idea that is attracting growing attention and support could directly mitigate this problem: a job guarantee. In its most ambitious form, such a program would ensure that anyone who wants work is guaranteed a meaningful, decently paid job. By creating a public option for employment, its supporters argue, a job guarantee could protect millions of people from the financial and psychological damage of joblessness and mobilize a vast labor force to tackle urgent societal problems, from infrastructure and climate adaptation to elder care and childcare. The concept of a job guarantee has a long history, both as an ideal and an actual policy. Article 23 of the 1948 Universal Declaration of Human Rights states: “Everyone has the right to work, to free choice of employment, to just and favourable conditions of work and to protection against unemployment.” During the Great Depression in the 1930s, Franklin D Roosevelt established the Works Progress Administration (WPA), which employed millions of Americans in ambitious public works projects that constructed roads, bridges, sewers, playing fields and much more. More recently, France , India and Argentina are among the countries that have launched versions of a job guarantee. Though a job guarantee and universal basic income (UBI) are often grouped together, a recent global survey found greater support for job guarantees than UBIs. Polling of Americans by the Democratic strategist David Shor also shows the same pattern , with greater support for the creation of well-paid jobs than for direct income support. This makes sense, the venture capitalist and civic activist Nick Hanauer said, because “jobs represent so much more than income in human societies. They represent connection and dignity and enfranchisement and participation.” Algernon Austin, director for race and economic justice at the Center for Economic and Policy Research, agreed: “A job guarantee is significantly preferable to UBI because work is more than just income. When you have a job, you gain work experience and you gain skills and you gain a network.” Calculating the cost of a job guarantee depends on a holistic assessment of its impacts. During a US Senate hearing on affordability in June, John Kennedy, a Republican senator for Louisiana, suggested that a job guarantee would cost trillions of dollars and was impossible. When Dr Julie Margetta Morgan, president of the public policy thinktank the Century Foundation, told Kennedy that she supported a federal job guarantee, he replied : “Do you believe in the Easter bunny?” Economists who study job guarantees see the calculation of costs and benefits differently. Max Kasy, a professor of economics at Oxford who has studied a recent job guarantee experiment in Austria, said that while the wages a job guarantee pays participants comprise a cost, such programs also save money in multiple ways. “The cost saving comes from the fact that you don’t have to pay unemployment benefits, or maybe disability benefits or early retirement benefits. Then people who are working pay taxes and make social insurance contributions, so that’s additional revenue for the state. And then they hopefully do something that’s actually useful for society,” he said. Participants in the job guarantee experiment in Austria also experienced social and psychological benefits . While the monetary value of greater wellbeing may be hard to quantify, such intangibles are crucial, according to Pavlina Tcherneva, a professor of economics at Bard College. “Providing a good job to a person is absolutely transformative,” she said. Factoring in the costs of health problems that come from precarious unemployment and long-term unemployment, she added, makes the policy even more attractive, saying: “It’s not only affordable, it’s an investment.” In September, the US representative Ayanna Pressley, a Democrat from Massachusetts, reintroduced a congressional resolution calling for the creation of a federal job guarantee, something she first proposed in 2021. Her proposal would create a federally funded but locally administered job guarantee that pays participants at least $25 an hour, with regular adjustments to reflect the rising cost of living. The jobs would include a range of sectors, such as emergency preparedness, relief and recovery after natural disasters, care for children and seniors, and public art projects modelled on the WPA’s popular Federal Art Project. Another recent proposal would directly tax AI companies to fund a federal job guarantee. The plan, which is supported by Democratic US representatives Greg Casar of Texas, Valerie Foushee of North Carolina and Sara Jacobs of California, would tax large AI companies on whatever was higher: the value of their “tokens” – units of data used in AI models – or their revenue from AI products. If the unemployment rate rose, the tax rate would increase. “AI CEOs are openly predicting their technology could put millions of Americans out of work, and our government is doing nothing to save jobs and protect working people,” Casar said in a written statement. In Cleveland, Ohio, a non-profit called Universal Basic Employment (UBE) is launching a small pilot study with a cohort of five workers who drive vans at a transportation company. Rather than create new jobs from scratch, the program subsidizes the wages of existing private-sector jobs in a way that benefits both workers and employers, according to Devin Cotten, founder and CEO of UBE. Cotten and his team wanted workers to make what they call an autonomous wage – the pay level at which people are no longer eligible for most social safety net benefits. In Cleveland, that was just over $27 per hour. At a cost of almost half a million dollars for one year, UBE’s pilot will split that $27 figure with employers. The drivers currently make about $15 an hour, so the employer will save money, and the workers will get a sizable raise. The program is not meant to replace other forms of assistance such as housing vouchers, Cotten said. But workers receiving more money as wages, rather than as a siloed benefit, can build their credit, perhaps qualify for a mortgage and also keep dollars circulating in the local economy, helping to revitalize poor neighborhoods. Such a model may even attract a broader base of political support. “Work is a shared value across political lines,” Cotten said. “I think crafting a solution based on work allows us to be a bipartisan solution.” Explore more on these topics AI (artificial intelligence) US work & careers US economy US politics Employment Economics analysis Share Reuse this content Most viewed Most viewed Business Economics Diversity & equality in business Small business Retail

https://www.theguardian.com/politics/202.text: Henry Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton. Photograph: Family handout/PA View image in fullscreen Henry Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton. Photograph: Family handout/PA Shabana Mahmood Shabana Mahmood launches review into murder of student Henry Nowak Move comes after claims that killer had history of using threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons Rajeev Syal Home affairs editor Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.30 EDT Last modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.51 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, has launched a review to examine whether opportunities were missed to prevent the murder of the student Henry Nowak. It follows claims that there were several warning signs that the perpetrator, Vickrum Digwa, had a history of threatening behaviour and an obsession with weapons. Nowak, 18, died in December after being fatally stabbed as he walked home from a night out in Southampton . He was handcuffed by police officers while bleeding to death after Digwa falsely accused Nowak of racial abuse. In police body-worn camera footage which prompted a public outcry, Nowak was heard repeatedly saying: “I’ve been stabbed,” to which an officer replied: “Don’t think you have, mate.” Nowak’s death sparked widespread protests, allegations of “two-tier policing” and a spike in racist attacks against the UK’s Sikh community. Digwa, a Sikh, was carrying two knives, including a kirpan, on the night of the killing. Carrying the blade is permitted in the UK for religious purposes. Digwa, 23, has subsequently been accused by young local Sikhs of using threatening behaviour in a Southampton gurdwara, or temple, in the months leading up to the fatal attack on Nowak. The Sun reported that Digwa was seen brandishing an airgun in his back garden in October 2022. A neighbour who recorded him firing shots said she reported this to the police, but Hampshire constabulary was unable to find a record of the incident. Speaking in the Commons, Mahmood said the review would be led by the former Conservative lord chancellor Alex Chalk KC and would report its initial findings within five months. “Last December, Henry Nowak’s life was cut short in a horrific and senseless act of violence. My thoughts today are with Henry’s family and his friends, who have shown extraordinary courage and dignity,” she said. “It [the review] will investigate what was known about the perpetrator, including any missed opportunities to intervene. “It will look at the Nowak family’s experience of the criminal justice system and whether they were supported in the manner they should have been. “Once the Independent Office for Police Conduct [IOPC] has concluded its investigation into the police response, this review will also consider the actions of the IOPC and, if necessary, the police.” Two officers, who were the first to arrive on the scene, are being investigated by the IOPC for potential gross misconduct. The investigation is looking at why they did not recognise that Nowak needed urgent medical attention and at the decision to arrest him rather than provide first aid. skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Nowak’s family welcomed the review as a “significant moment” in their fight for justice. “Since Henry was murdered, we’ve fought tirelessly for answers to questions no family should ever have to ask. The emotional toll of that fight, on top of the unimaginable grief of losing Henry, has been immense,” the family said. “We hope this review, alongside the ongoing investigations and inquest, will finally uncover the full truth and deliver the accountability and meaningful change we have fought so hard for. “Our experience of the criminal justice system has been deeply disappointing, and we are determined that no other family should have to endure what we have.” Digwa was jailed for life with a minimum term of 21 years. He has been given permission to challenge the length of that sentence at the court of appeal on 5 November. Kiran Kaur, Digwa’s mother, was also jailed for three years for assisting an offender after she removed the knife used by her son. The knife was found by police at their family home along with more than 20 other weapons.
